headline: Medium-risk shared-state and output-trust issues: LangGraph can write shared graph state while RisingWave is a non-networked data system, creating default-path leakage and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can read/write application-defined files and uses shared checkpointer state across instances, so attacker-controlled content can enter its graph state and be reinterpreted as instructions. RisingWave is non-networked, so the main pathway is through LangGraph’s shared state rather than direct agent-to-agent messaging. The interaction is plausible in default orchestration setups, but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents are wired to the same checkpointer or shared workspace, injected content can cross from one run to the other.
IF LangGraph nodes parse stored graph state as instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer execution.
mitigations: Separate per-agent workspaces and checkpointer namespaces.
Add provenance tags to all shared state entries.
Treat all persisted state as untrusted input.
requires-engineering: add content filtering before any instruction parsing.
Run a quick red-team test with a malicious state payload.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph explicitly reads and writes filesystem-backed application files and handles model-provider API keys, while RisingWave is documented as non-networked. If they share a workspace, data touched by LangGraph can be exposed through shared files or persisted state; RisingWave does not add outbound leakage, so the risk is workspace-mediated rather than exfiltration-heavy.
conditions: IF the two systems share an OS workspace, files written by LangGraph can be read by the other side.
IF sensitive graph state is persisted in the shared checkpointer, later runs can recover it.
mitigations: Use separate directories and credentials per agent.
Store secrets outside shared graph state.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
requires-engineering: encrypt persisted state at rest.
Audit shared files for sensitive fields before reuse.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LangGraph has filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and broad network egress; RisingWave is a data-engineering system with no declared concurrency controls here. If both are pointed at the same mutable resources, writes can conflict even though RisingWave’s write surfaces are not enumerated. Uncertainty about RisingWave’s exact mutation surfaces pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, database, or stream, concurrent writes can race.
IF no external locking is configured, one agent can overwrite the other’s state.
mitigations: Assign disjoint mutable resources.
Enable external locking around shared writes.
Serialize write phases manually.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks.
Review any shared database or git-like state before running.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph can produce graph outputs that downstream nodes or tools may treat as authoritative, and RisingWave is a data-processing system that can propagate upstream mistakes into materialized outputs. Because the pair lacks explicit verification or guardrails in the profiles, a bad LangGraph output can cascade into incorrect downstream data products. The pathway is plausible in default orchestration, but not directly observed.
conditions: IF RisingWave consumes LangGraph-produced records without validation, errors can propagate into downstream tables or views.
IF LangGraph nodes emit unverified facts, later stages may act on them as ground truth.
mitigations: Insert schema validation between stages.
Require human review for high-impact outputs.
Add checksum or provenance fields to records.
requires-engineering: implement end-to-end verification gates.
Replay one sample pipeline with known-bad input.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent. LangGraph is open-source orchestration software and RisingWave is a non-networked open-source data system, so compliance risk is limited to whatever the operator configures. The other agent is not separately cited because no concrete compliance surface is exposed in its profile.
conditions: IF the operator routes regulated data through a noncompliant deployment, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF retention settings differ across shared storage, deletion requests may not propagate uniformly.
mitigations: Document data classes before deployment.
Set explicit retention and deletion procedures.
Keep regulated data out of shared state.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement checks.
Review deployment region and vendor contracts.
